what: AGCO makes agricultural machinery: tractors, combine harvesters, planters, sprayers and the guidance and precision-farming technology that goes with them. Its main brands are Fendt, Massey Ferguson, Valtra and the PTx precision agriculture range.
customers: Farmers and agricultural contractors worldwide, sold through independent dealers. Europe and South America are more important to AGCO than to its American rivals.
money: Fendt and Valtra tractors and harvesting equipment, the most profitable region.
Massey Ferguson equipment and PTx precision farming products.
South America and rest of world
Equipment for Brazilian and Argentine row-crop farming and other markets.
moat: Fendt is a genuine premium brand in European farming, commanding higher prices for better technology, and dealer networks for farm equipment take decades to build. The precision agriculture products are designed to work on equipment from any manufacturer, which widens the addressable market beyond AGCO's own machines.
risks: Farm equipment is deeply cyclical and is in a downturn. Revenue fell from $14.4B in 2023 to $10.1B, a decline of nearly 30%.
Farmer income depends on crop prices, which have been weak, and farmers postpone buying machines when margins are thin.
Large exposure to Brazil and Argentina adds currency and political risk.
Debt of about $2.6B against $861.8M of cash must be serviced through the trough of the cycle.
The shares trade at about 26 times earnings, which looks expensive until you remember that earnings are at a cyclical low.
opportunities: Cyclical troughs in farm equipment have historically been followed by multi-year recoveries, and used equipment inventories eventually clear.
The precision agriculture business carries higher margins than machinery and grows with the adoption of guidance, spraying and data systems.
Fendt's European premium position is the most profitable part of the group and continues to take share.
Fifteen analysts average a $124.67 target, about 21% above the current price.
watch: Dealer inventory levels. In farm equipment, the recovery begins when dealers have worked off excess stock, not when farmers feel better, so inventory is the leading indicator of the next upcycle.
